questions.stem: Roger Sinclair, 70, has had a hot, swollen, red left knee for 20 hours, with fevers and rigors overnight. You see him in general practice. When you ask about trauma he says, "I haven't fallen on it or injured my knee at all." Which question should you ask next to find out how bacteria could have got into the joint?
options: Have you ever had a sudden hot, swollen joint or a painful big toe before?
Have you had any diarrhoea, or red or sore eyes, in the past month?
Have you had any cut, scratch or puncture to the skin of that knee lately?
Do you take any fluid tablets, or drink alcohol most days?
questions.why: Patients often don't count a small puncture as an injury. Asking directly about breaks in the skin is what uncovers direct inoculation, here a dirty nail knelt on 2 days earlier, as the route into the joint.
notes: This screens for gout, a crystal differential. It doesn't find a way for bacteria to get into the joint.
This screens for reactive arthritis, which follows a gut or genitourinary infection. It doesn't find a way for bacteria to get into the joint.
Diuretics and alcohol are risk factors for gout. This question doesn't find a way for bacteria to get into the joint.

questions.stem: Mr Sinclair, 70, is in general practice with a hot, swollen left knee and a likely septic arthritis after a nail puncture. His temperature has risen from 38.4 to 38.7 °C with a rigor. Now HR 108, BP 134/80, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, and he is alert. He cannot bear weight. What is the most appropriate management now?
options: Give IV flucloxacillin 2 g in the practice now, then send him to hospital
Same-day hospital transfer by ambulance for aspiration; withhold antibiotics
Start oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly and review him in the practice tomorrow
Request CRP, urate and knee X-ray today and review results with him tomorrow
questions.why: Suspected septic arthritis is an emergency that needs same-day hospital care. With no shock or organ dysfunction, hold antibiotics until the joint has been aspirated (with blood cultures) so the organism can be identified. Keep him nil by mouth in case he needs a washout.
notes: Giving antibiotics before aspiration can make the synovial culture negative. Give them first only if there are signs of shock or organ dysfunction, and he has none.
Oral antibiotics and outpatient review undertreat a joint-destroying emergency, and starting them before aspiration hides the organism.
Outpatient tests delay definitive diagnosis. Blood tests and an X-ray cannot rule septic arthritis in or out, and the cartilage can be destroyed within days.

questions.stem: Mr Sinclair, 70, has a septic left knee with a large effusion. He sits holding the knee bent at about 20–30°, supported on a pillow, and resists any attempt to straighten or bend it further. What is the main reason this position is the most comfortable?
options: Joint capsule volume is greatest, so intra-articular pressure is lowest
Reflex quadriceps inhibition leaves the hamstrings unopposed in flexion
The collateral ligaments are tightest, so the inflamed joint is stabilised
Synovial blood flow falls in flexion, so less exudate forms in the joint
questions.why: The knee capsule holds the most fluid at about 20–30° of flexion. In that position the pressure inside the joint, and so the stretch on the inflamed, richly innervated capsule, is lowest. Full extension or deeper flexion raises the pressure and the pain.
notes: Muscle inhibition does happen, but it doesn't explain why he holds the knee still at this angle. The main reason is lower capsular pressure.
The collateral ligaments are tight in extension and slack in flexion, so this has it the wrong way round.
Flexion doesn't usefully reduce synovial exudate. The comfort comes from lower pressure inside the joint, not from less fluid being made.

questions.stem: Examining Mr Sinclair's left knee, you find a tense swelling that extends about a hand's breadth above the upper border of the patella. The bulge test and patellar tap are positive. Which structure, continuous with the knee joint cavity, accounts for the swelling above the patella?
questions.why: The suprapatellar bursa (pouch) runs up deep to quadriceps and connects with the knee joint, so a joint effusion fills it and bulges above the patella. It is also the space the needle enters in the usual superolateral approach to aspirating the knee.
notes: The prepatellar bursa lies between the skin and the patella and does not connect with the joint. It swells over the front of the kneecap, not above it.
The superficial infrapatellar bursa lies over the patellar tendon, below the patella. It does not connect with the joint, so it can't explain swelling above the patella.
The pes anserinus bursa is on the upper medial tibia, deep to the sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus tendons. It is separate from the joint.
